query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: An enhanced thermodynamic integration scheme that employs tailored collective variables to capture multi-component solid‐liquid coexistence will accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, and volume change at melting for high‐entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-component high-entropy alloy in its near-melting solid state with inherent chemical disorder.
generation.intervention: Apply an enhanced free-energy integration method that uses advanced sampling techniques (e.g., metadynamics or umbrella sampling) with collective variables designed to account for the structural rearrangements during melting.
generation.conditions: High-temperature simulation conditions straddling the solid-liquid coexistence regime, with validation under comparable experimental conditions such as DSC or in situ high-temperature microscopy.
generation.structural_mediator: Tailored collective variables that capture the local atomic rearrangements and phase coexistence at the solid-liquid interface.
generation.mechanism: By directing sampling along key order parameters that describe the transition, the method reduces the convergence time for free energy differences and minimizes errors related to the vast configurational space, thus yielding improved estimates of melting properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The method is expected to predict melting temperatures within approximately 5-10% of experimental values, along with reliable estimates of fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting, while significantly reducing computational effort compared to conventional calorimetric or first-principles approaches.
generation.baseline: Traditional DSC measurements and standard first-principles free-energy methods, which are either experimentally intensive or computationally expensive, particularly for the compositional complexity of HEAs.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable mainly to HEA systems that exhibit a well-defined solid-liquid coexistence. Its accuracy may diminish for compositions with extremely broad or diffuse phase boundaries or for systems where the tailored collective variables are less effective.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative improvement in computational efficiency and the precise error bounds on predicted thermodynamic quantities depend on the optimal choice and tuning of the collective variables, which may require further systematic validation for different HEA compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform parallel studies on a set of representative high-entropy alloys. First, use the enhanced thermodynamic integration method with tailored collective variables to compute the free energy changes associated with melting. Then, experimentally determine the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change using high-resolution techniques such as DSC and in situ high-temperature microscopy. Compare the simulation outputs with experimental measurements for multiple HEA compositions.
measurements: Melting temperature (Tm) from both simulation and DSC
Fusion enthalpy (ΔHfusion) and fusion entropy (ΔSfusion) via free energy integration and calorimetric measurements
Volume change at melting measured via dilatometry or comparable in situ techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulation predictions for any of the thermodynamic properties (Tm, ΔHfusion, ΔSfusion, or volume change) deviate by more than 10% relative error from the experimental benchmark values for at least three distinct HEA compositions, the enhanced free-energy integration method would be considered falsified for this application.

cited_evidence.text:
The LSF methodology proposed by Dong et al . [29] , [30] was adopted to describe the finite-temperature magnetic state of each alloy species in PM CoCrFeMnNi HEA. The root-mean-square magnetic moment m I ( w , T ) [30] , which is formulated as m I = ∫ μ 2 ⋅ x ( μ ) d μ with x ( μ ) being the spin-density distribution of longitudinal magnetic component μ , was used to represent the LSF energetics at thermal excitations in both the fcc and hcp phases. For the sake of computational feasibility of determining { m I }, we used the ‘fluctuating medium approximation’ and the ‘one shot from static equilibrium approach’ [29] . The present LSF methodology has been applied to PM bcc and fcc Fe and Fe-Cr-Ni alloy, and the predicted finite-temperature properties such as single-crystal elastic constants [29] , [30] , lattice expansion [34] and intrinsic energy barriers [39] confirm the accurate description of the magnetic state at elevated temperatures.

The finite-temperature properties were derived from the free energy F α ( α represents the fcc or hcp phase) by accounting for lattice expansion and LSFs at finite temperature, which is expressed as F α ( w , T ) = E int ( w , { M I }) − TS mag
